AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.1 · Classify
        Chemical bonds
        Name two elements. Can you say how they will bond, and what the substance will do, before you ever see it?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Same chlorine. Two partners. Two different worlds.
        Sodium is a soft metal that fizzes on water. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Together they make table salt: a white crystal that stays solid until 801 °C. Swap sodium for hydrogen and chlorine makes hydrogen chloride, which stays a gas until it is cooled below −85 °C.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  What decides whether chlorine ends up in a high-melting crystal or in a gas?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Whether its partner is a metal or a non-metal
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          How heavy its partner’s atoms are
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          How reactive its partner is
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          How many chlorine atoms join on

Atoms bond because a full outer shell is more stable, and there are only three ways to get one. A metal atom has one, two or three outer electrons and gives them away. A non-metal atom has four to seven and takes more in, or shares.
        Metal with non-metal: electrons are transferred, the atoms become oppositely charged ions, and the ions attract. That is ionic bonding. Two non-metals: neither gives way, so they share pairs of electrons. That is covalent bonding. Metal atoms on their own release their outer electrons into a sea that belongs to the whole lump. That is metallic bonding. So the first question is always the same: metal or non-metal?

The bond decider
            Pick two elements. Call the bond. Watch it form.
          
          0 pairs called
        
        Tap an element, then its partner. Tap the same element twice for the element on its own.
        
          
            
              Group 1
            
              Group 2
            
              
            
              Group 4
            
              Group 5
            
              Group 6
            
              Group 7
            
            
              H
            
              Li
            
              C
            
              N
            
              O
            
              F
            
              Na
            
              Mg
            
              S
            
              Cl
            
              K
            
              Ca
            
              Cu
            
          
          Part of the periodic table, by group. Most transition metals and Group 3 are left out.
        
        No pair yet

The bond decides what the substance does. Ionic compounds and metals are giant structures, held by strong attraction all the way through, so they melt only when very hot. Covalent substances split two ways. Most are small molecules that melt and boil at low temperatures; a few, like diamond and sand, are giant networks that melt only when very hot. To carry a current you need charged particles that can move: a metal's electron sea always can, but ions only can once the solid melts or dissolves.

!Think again
        “Ice melts at 0 °C and salt at 801 °C, so the covalent bonds in water must be weak.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  What is wrong with that reasoning?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Nothing. A low melting point means weak bonds.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Melting separates whole water molecules from each other. The weak forces are between molecules; the O–H bonds inside each one stay intact.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Covalent bonds are weak, but they break only when water boils, not when it melts.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The bonds do break, but they re-form straight away in the liquid.

Sort it
  Ionic, covalent or metallic?
  Eight substances. Decide from the elements in each, not from what you remember about it.
  Tap a card, then tap the box it belongs in. Tap a placed card to take it back.
  
    
      NH₃
    
      MgO
    
      HCl
    
      CaCl₂
    
      CO₂
    
      Brass (copper with zinc)
    
      Na, a lump of sodium
    
      KBr
    
    
  
  
    
      
        Ionic 
        
      
    
      
        Covalent 
        
      
    
      
        Metallic 
        
      
    
  
  
    Check the sort

Command words in this lesson
        
          IdentifyName it. One word or a short phrase is enough.
          PredictGive a likely outcome. Here, say which elements are metals.
          DeduceReach a conclusion from the data you are given.
          JustifyBack your answer with evidence from the question.

Key fact
        Metal with non-metal: ionic, electrons transferred. Non-metal with non-metal: covalent, electrons shared. Metal on its own or with other metals: metallic, electrons delocalised.

Examiner tip
        When a question says "predict" or "identify" the bonding, justify it from the elements: metal + non-metal → ionic, two non-metals → covalent, a metal alone → metallic. Naming the bond type without saying why the elements produce it rarely earns full marks.

Exam ladder
        Four rungs, one point each. Every question shows its command word and what it is worth in the exam.
      
      
        0 of 4 rungs tried
        Scored when all four are done.
      
    
    

      
        
          Rung 1 · Recall
          Predict
          1 mark
        
        
        Water (H₂O) is made from two non-metals. Predict the type of bonding it contains.
        
          
            
              
                
                  
                  
                  A
                
                Ionic — because water can conduct electricity
              
            
          
            
              
                
                  
                  
                  B
                
                Metallic — the atoms share a sea of delocalised electrons
              
            
          
            
              
                
                  
                  
                  C
                
                Ionic — one atom transfers electrons to the other
              
            
          
            
              
                
                  
                  
                  D
                
                Covalent — the non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons
              
            
          
        
        
      

      
        
          Rung 2 · Apply
          Deduce
          3 marks
        
        SubstancePQRMelting point / °C1085−114801Solid conducts?yesnonoMolten conducts?yesnoyes
        Use the data in the table. Deduce the type of bonding in each substance.
        
        
        
          
            
              
                Substance P
                
                  ioniccovalent (small molecules)metallic
                
              
            
              
                Substance Q
                
                  ioniccovalent (small molecules)metallic
                
              
            
              
                Substance R
                
                  ioniccovalent (small molecules)metallic
                
              
            
          
        
        
          Check my answer
        
        
      

      
        
          Rung 3 · Explain
          Explain
          3 marks
        
        
          
  
  Potassium reacts with bromine to make potassium bromide, KBr. Explain why the bonding in potassium bromide is ionic. Put the links in order.
  3 links belong. 2 do not.

  
    
      The links
      
        
          The ionic bond is the transfer of the electron.
        
          Each potassium atom loses one electron to a bromine atom, making K⁺ and Br⁻ ions.
        
          The oppositely charged ions attract. That strong electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.
        
          Potassium and bromine share a pair of electrons.
        
          Potassium is a metal and bromine is a non-metal, so electrons are transferred rather than shared.

Key note · AQA 5.2.1.1
        Chemical bonds
      
      
        Cover and recall
        
      
    
    
      
        
          01
          Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, like a noble gas.
          
        
      
        
          02
          Metal + non-metal: ionic. The metal transfers electrons; the ions attract.
          
        
      
        
          03
          Non-metal + non-metal: covalent. The atoms share pairs of electrons.
          
        
      
        
          04
          Metal alone or in an alloy: metallic. Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
          
        
      
        
          05
          Hydrogen is a non-metal, even though it sits above Group 1.
          
        
      
        
          06
          Justify every prediction from the elements: say which ones are metals.
          
        
      
    
    Photograph this card. Tomorrow, cover it and say each line first.

Practice set · Triple Higher
        Every question from this lesson
      
      0 of 12 answered · 0 matched the mark scheme
    
    
      
        
          1
          
            Sodium chloride is made from a metal and a non-metal. Predict the type of bonding it contains and describe how it forms.
            
              
                AHydrogen bonding — a weak attraction forms between the two atoms
              
                BMetallic — the atoms sit in a sea of delocalised electrons
              
                CCovalent — the metal and non-metal share a pair of electrons
              
                DIonic — the metal atom transfers electrons to the non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions that attract
              
            
            
          
        
      
        
          2
          
            Magnesium (Group 2) reacts with oxygen (Group 6) to form magnesium oxide. Identify the type of bonding in MgO.
            
              
                AIonic — magnesium transfers 2 electrons to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions
              
                BNo bonding — both are stable so they do not react
              
                CCovalent — they share 2 electrons to fill their outer shells
              
                DMetallic — magnesium releases electrons into a sea
              
            
            
          
        
      
        
          3
          
            Water (H₂O) is made from two non-metals. Predict the type of bonding it contains.
            
              
                AIonic — because water can conduct electricity
              
                BMetallic — the atoms share a sea of delocalised electrons
              
                CIonic — one atom transfers electrons to the other
              
                DCovalent — the non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons
              
            
            
          
        
      
        
          4
          
            Explain why copper is described as having metallic bonding.
            
              
                AIts atoms are simply packed closely together with no forces between them
              
                BIts atoms share pairs of electrons in covalent bonds
              
                CIt transfers electrons to form positive and negative ions
              
                DIts atoms release outer electrons into a delocalised sea, and the positive ions are attracted to that sea

Real bonding is a sliding scale and a few metal compounds, such as aluminium chloride, behave covalently; GCSE questions avoid them. Dot-and-cross figures show outer shells only for covalent molecules and full shells for ions.

Start here
        Same chlorine. Two partners. Two different worlds.
        Sodium is a soft metal that fizzes on water. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Together they make table salt: a white crystal that stays solid until 801 °C.           B
          How heavy its partner’s atoms are
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          How reactive its partner is
        
      
    
      
        
          D

Atoms bond because a full outer shell is more stable, and there are only three ways to get one. A metal atom has one, two or three outer electrons and gives them away. A non-metal atom has four to seven and takes more in, or shares.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.2 · Process
        Ionic bonding
        A soft metal and a poisonous gas become the salt on your chips. Where do the electrons go, and what actually holds the salt together?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Hot sodium, a jar of chlorine, a flash of yellow light.
        Drop hot sodium into chlorine gas and it burns with a bright yellow flame. When the smoke clears, the jar is coated in white crystals of sodium chloride. A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell. A chlorine atom has seven.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Where does sodium's single outer electron end up?
  
    
      
        
          A
          It moves across to the chlorine atom
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The two atoms share it between them
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          It stays on sodium; the atoms just stick
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          It is given off as the yellow light

A full outer shell is stable: that is why the noble gases barely react. Sodium (2.8.1) is one electron past a full shell; chlorine (2.8.7) is one short. When a metal meets a non-metal, the metal atom loses its outer electrons and the non-metal atom gains them. Both end up with the electron arrangement of a noble gas. Neither is an atom any more: each is an ion, a particle with a charge. Watch it happen, one step at a time, and call each step before you see it.

Worked · call each step
            Sodium and chlorine
          
          
            
              Na + Cl
            
              Mg + O
            
          
        
        NaClNa 2.8.1Cl 2.8.7
        Before · two neutral atoms, crosses for Na, dots for Cl
        
          
            Step 1 of 3 · Which atom will lose electrons?
            
              
                Sodium
              
                Chlorine
              
                Neither: they share a pair

The charge on an ion comes from counting electrons. A Group 1 metal loses one, so it becomes 1+. Group 2 loses two: 2+. A Group 7 non-metal gains one: 1−. Group 6 gains two: 2−. The ions are held by strong electrostatic forces acting in every direction, which is why ionic compounds are giant lattices, not pairs. Now draw one yourself.

Start here

    Commit first

          B

          C

          D

A full outer shell is stable: that is why the noble gases barely react. Sodium (2.8.1) is one electron past a full shell; chlorine (2.8.7) is one short. Neither is an atom any more: each is an ion, a particle with a charge. Watch it happen, one step at a time, and call each step before you see it.

            Sodium and chlorine
          
          
            
              Na + Cl
            
              Mg + O
            
          
        
        NaClNa 2.8.1Cl 2.8.7

                Sodium
              
                Chlorine

          D

A full outer shell is stable: that is why the noble gases barely react. Sodium (2.8.1) is one electron past a full shell; chlorine (2.8.7) is one short. AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.2 · Process
        Ionic bonding
        A soft metal and a poisonous gas become the salt on your chips. Where do the electrons go, and what actually holds the salt together?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Hot sodium, a jar of chlorine, a flash of yellow light.
        Drop hot sodium into chlorine gas and it burns with a bright yellow flame. When the smoke clears, the jar is coated in white crystals of sodium chloride. A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell. A chlorine atom has seven.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Where does sodium's single outer electron end up?
  
    
      
        
          A
          It moves across to the chlorine atom
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The two atoms share it between them
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          It stays on sodium; the atoms just stick
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          It is given off as the yellow light

A full outer shell is stable: that is why the noble gases barely react. Sodium (2.8.1) is one electron past a full shell; chlorine (2.8.7) is one short. When a metal meets a non-metal, the metal atom loses its outer electrons and the non-metal atom gains them. Both end up with the electron arrangement of a noble gas. Neither is an atom any more: each is an ion, a particle with a charge. Watch it happen, one step at a time, and call each step before you see it.

Worked · call each step
            Sodium and chlorine
          
          
            
              Na + Cl
            
              Mg + O
            
          
        
        NaClNa 2.8.1Cl 2.8.7
        Before · two neutral atoms, crosses for Na, dots for Cl
        
          
            Step 1 of 3 · Which atom will lose electrons?
            
              
                Sodium
              
                Chlorine
              
                Neither: they share a pair

The charge on an ion comes from counting electrons. A Group 1 metal loses one, so it becomes 1+. Group 2 loses two: 2+. A Group 7 non-metal gains one: 1−. Group 6 gains two: 2−. The ions are held by strong electrostatic forces acting in every direction, which is why ionic compounds are giant lattices, not pairs. Now draw one yourself.

sections.text:
AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.3 · Model
        Ionic compounds
        The formula says NaCl. So is a grain of salt made of little NaCl molecules, or of something else entirely?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Crush a salt crystal. You get smaller cubes.
        Look at table salt through a hand lens and every grain is a tiny cube with flat faces and square corners. Crush one and the fragments break along flat faces into smaller cubes. Grow salt slowly from a solution and you get cubes the size of dice.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does salt come out as cubes at every size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The particles inside stack in one regular pattern that repeats
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Salt molecules are shaped like tiny cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Factories cut salt into cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Water shapes the grains as it evaporates

When sodium reacts with chlorine, the ions do not pair off. Each Na⁺ pulls on every Cl⁻ near it, and each Cl⁻ pulls on every Na⁺. They settle into a giant ionic lattice: a regular, three-dimensional arrangement in which positive and negative ions alternate in every direction. The strong electrostatic forces act in all directions at once. “Giant” means exactly that: a single grain holds around 10¹⁸ ions, and the pattern repeats the whole way through. The cube you see is the repeat you cannot.

The lattice lens
            How many neighbours does one ion have?
          
          1 of 3 views
        
        
          
            Commit first. In a real salt crystal, how many chloride ions sit right next to one sodium ion?
            
              2468

!Think again
        “The formula is NaCl, so salt is made of NaCl molecules: one sodium stuck to one chlorine.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  You have just counted six neighbours. What does the formula NaCl really tell you?
  
    
      
        
          A
          There are exactly as many Na⁺ ions as Cl⁻ ions in the whole lattice: a 1 : 1 ratio, not a molecule.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Each Na⁺ is bonded to one particular Cl⁻; the other five are just close by.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The lattice is made of NaCl molecules packed together in a cube.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Nothing: NaCl molecules form first and then join up into a crystal.

Deduce the formula from the diagram
        Count the ions. Write the simplest ratio.
        The exam shows part of a lattice and asks for the empirical formula. Count each kind of ion in the diagram, then cancel down. Type the formula with plain numbers, for example Na2O.
        
          Compound 1Compound 2Compound 3
        
        Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻
        
          Empirical formula
          
          Check

No drawing of a lattice is the real thing. A dot-and-cross diagram shows where the electrons went but not the lattice. A 2D diagram shows the alternating pattern but only one layer. A ball-and-stick model shows the 3D repeat but draws the ions far apart and joins them with sticks, as if the force ran along a line. Every model trades one truth for another. AQA asks you to say which.

Na+Cl−Na+  2.8Cl−  2.8.8A · dot-and-cross
          Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻B · 2D lattice
          C · ball-and-stick
        
        
  Sort the limitations
  Which model has this limitation?
  Each statement is a limitation of exactly one of the three models above.
  Tap a card, then tap the box it belongs in. Tap a placed card to take it back.
  
    
      Gives no idea of the crystal being three-dimensional.
    
      Shows a single layer, so each ion seems to have four neighbours, not six.
    
      Leaves big gaps between ions that really touch.
    
      Suggests each ion belongs with one partner.
    
      Shows only one pair of ions, not the giant lattice they are part of.
    
      Draws sticks, as if each force acts along one line to one neighbour.
    
    
  
  
    
      
        A · dot-and-cross 
        
      
    
      
        B · 2D lattice 
        
      
    
      
        C · ball-and-stick 
        
      
    
  
  
    Check the sort

Command words in this lesson
        
          DescribeGive the features: regular, 3D, alternating, forces in all directions.
          DeduceReach the formula from the diagram you are given. Show the count.
          EvaluateGive strengths and limitations, then judge.

Key fact
        An ionic compound is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions. Its formula is the simplest ratio of ions, not a molecule.

Examiner tip
        For conduction marks you must say the ions are free to move. Solid ionic compounds don't conduct because the ions are locked in the lattice; only when molten or dissolved can the ions move and carry charge. "It contains charged particles" on its own scores nothing.

        Count the ions. Write the simplest ratio.
        The exam shows part of a lattice and asks for the empirical formula. Count each kind of ion in the diagram, then cancel down. Type the formula with plain numbers, for example Na2O.
        
          Compound 1Compound 2Compound 3
        
        Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻
        
          Empirical formula
          
          Check

No drawing of a lattice is the real thing. A dot-and-cross diagram shows where the electrons went but not the lattice. A 2D diagram shows the alternating pattern but only one layer. A ball-and-stick model shows the 3D repeat but draws the ions far apart and joins them with sticks, as if the force ran along a line. Every model trades one truth for another. AQA asks you to say which.

Na+Cl−Na+  2.8Cl−  2.8.8A · dot-and-cross
          Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻B · 2D lattice
          C · ball-and-stick
        
        
  Sort the limitations
  Which model has this limitation?
  Each statement is a limitation of exactly one of the three models above.
  Tap a card, then tap the box it belongs in. Tap a placed card to take it back.
  
    
      Gives no idea of the crystal being three-dimensional.
    
      Shows a single layer, so each ion seems to have four neighbours, not six.
    
      Leaves big gaps between ions that really touch.
    
      Suggests each ion belongs with one partner.
    
      Shows only one pair of ions, not the giant lattice they are part of.
    
      Draws sticks, as if each force acts along one line to one neighbour.
    
    
  
  
    
      
        A · dot-and-cross 
        
      
    
      
        B · 2D lattice 
        
      
    
      
        C · ball-and-stick 
        
      
    
  
  
    Check the sort

Command words in this lesson
        
          DescribeGive the features: regular, 3D, alternating, forces in all directions.
          DeduceReach the formula from the diagram you are given. Show the count.
          EvaluateGive strengths and limitations, then judge.

Key fact
        An ionic compound is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions. Its formula is the simplest ratio of ions, not a molecule.

Examiner tip
        For conduction marks you must say the ions are free to move. Solid ionic compounds don't conduct because the ions are locked in the lattice; only when molten or dissolved can the ions move and carry charge. "It contains charged particles" on its own scores nothing.

sections.text:
AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.3 · Model
        Ionic compounds
        The formula says NaCl. So is a grain of salt made of little NaCl molecules, or of something else entirely?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Crush a salt crystal. You get smaller cubes.
        Look at table salt through a hand lens and every grain is a tiny cube with flat faces and square corners. Crush one and the fragments break along flat faces into smaller cubes. Grow salt slowly from a solution and you get cubes the size of dice.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does salt come out as cubes at every size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The particles inside stack in one regular pattern that repeats
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Salt molecules are shaped like tiny cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Factories cut salt into cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Water shapes the grains as it evaporates

When sodium reacts with chlorine, the ions do not pair off. Each Na⁺ pulls on every Cl⁻ near it, and each Cl⁻ pulls on every Na⁺. They settle into a giant ionic lattice: a regular, three-dimensional arrangement in which positive and negative ions alternate in every direction. The strong electrostatic forces act in all directions at once. “Giant” means exactly that: a single grain holds around 10¹⁸ ions, and the pattern repeats the whole way through. The cube you see is the repeat you cannot.

The lattice lens
            How many neighbours does one ion have?
          
          1 of 3 views
        
        
          
            Commit first. In a real salt crystal, how many chloride ions sit right next to one sodium ion?
            
              2468

!Think again
        “The formula is NaCl, so salt is made of NaCl molecules: one sodium stuck to one chlorine.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  You have just counted six neighbours. What does the formula NaCl really tell you?
  
    
      
        
          A
          There are exactly as many Na⁺ ions as Cl⁻ ions in the whole lattice: a 1 : 1 ratio, not a molecule.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Each Na⁺ is bonded to one particular Cl⁻; the other five are just close by.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The lattice is made of NaCl molecules packed together in a cube.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Nothing: NaCl molecules form first and then join up into a crystal.

sections.text:
AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.3 · Model
        Ionic compounds
        The formula says NaCl. So is a grain of salt made of little NaCl molecules, or of something else entirely?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Crush a salt crystal. You get smaller cubes.
        Look at table salt through a hand lens and every grain is a tiny cube with flat faces and square corners. Crush one and the fragments break along flat faces into smaller cubes. Grow salt slowly from a solution and you get cubes the size of dice.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does salt come out as cubes at every size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The particles inside stack in one regular pattern that repeats
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Salt molecules are shaped like tiny cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Factories cut salt into cubes
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Water shapes the grains as it evaporates

When sodium reacts with chlorine, the ions do not pair off. Each Na⁺ pulls on every Cl⁻ near it, and each Cl⁻ pulls on every Na⁺. They settle into a giant ionic lattice: a regular, three-dimensional arrangement in which positive and negative ions alternate in every direction. The strong electrostatic forces act in all directions at once. “Giant” means exactly that: a single grain holds around 10¹⁸ ions, and the pattern repeats the whole way through. The cube you see is the repeat you cannot.

The lattice lens
            How many neighbours does one ion have?
          
          1 of 3 views
        
        
          
            Commit first. In a real salt crystal, how many chloride ions sit right next to one sodium ion?
            
              2468

!Think again
        “The formula is NaCl, so salt is made of NaCl molecules: one sodium stuck to one chlorine.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  You have just counted six neighbours. What does the formula NaCl really tell you?
  
    
      
        
          A
          There are exactly as many Na⁺ ions as Cl⁻ ions in the whole lattice: a 1 : 1 ratio, not a molecule.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Each Na⁺ is bonded to one particular Cl⁻; the other five are just close by.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The lattice is made of NaCl molecules packed together in a cube.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Nothing: NaCl molecules form first and then join up into a crystal.

Deduce the formula from the diagram
        Count the ions. Write the simplest ratio.
        The exam shows part of a lattice and asks for the empirical formula. Count each kind of ion in the diagram, then cancel down. Type the formula with plain numbers, for example Na2O.
        
          Compound 1Compound 2Compound 3
        
        Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺Mg²⁺O²⁻Mg²⁺O²⁻
        
          Empirical formula
          
          Check

No drawing of a lattice is the real thing. A dot-and-cross diagram shows where the electrons went but not the lattice. A 2D diagram shows the alternating pattern but only one layer. A ball-and-stick model shows the 3D repeat but draws the ions far apart and joins them with sticks, as if the force ran along a line. Every model trades one truth for another. AQA asks you to say which.

Na+Cl−Na+  2.8Cl−  2.8.8A · dot-and-cross
          Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻Na⁺Cl⁻B · 2D lattice
          C · ball-and-stick
        
        
  Sort the limitations
  Which model has this limitation?
  Each statement is a limitation of exactly one of the three models above.
  Tap a card, then tap the box it belongs in. Tap a placed card to take it back.
  
    
      Gives no idea of the crystal being three-dimensional.
    
      Shows a single layer, so each ion seems to have four neighbours, not six.
    
      Leaves big gaps between ions that really touch.
    
      Suggests each ion belongs with one partner.
    
      Shows only one pair of ions, not the giant lattice they are part of.
    
      Draws sticks, as if each force acts along one line to one neighbour.
    
    
  
  
    
      
        A · dot-and-cross 
        
      
    
      
        B · 2D lattice 
        
      
    
      
        C · ball-and-stick

AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.4 · Process
        Covalent bonding
        When two atoms both want electrons, neither will give any away. How do they still end up with full shells?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Two hydrogen atoms. One electron each. Both need two.
        Hydrogen gas is not made of single atoms. It is made of H₂ molecules, and pulling one apart takes a lot of energy. Yet each hydrogen atom has only one electron, and a full first shell needs two. Neither atom is a metal, so neither will hand its electron over.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  How can both hydrogen atoms have a full shell at the same time?
  
    
      
        
          A
          They share their two electrons, and both count the pair as their own
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          One gives its electron to the other, making ions
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          They borrow electrons from the air around them
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          They cannot: H₂ has half-empty shells

Two non-metal atoms overlap their outer shells and share a pair of electrons, one from each. Both atoms count the shared pair as their own. The pair sits between the two nuclei and is attracted to both of them, and that attraction holds the atoms together: one shared pair is one covalent bond. Covalent bonds are strong. An atom forms as many bonds as it needs electrons: hydrogen one, oxygen two, nitrogen three, carbon four. Call the next one before you see it.

Worked · water, H₂O
            Step 1 · count the outer electrons
          
          Step 1 of 3
        
        OHHO: 6 outer, needs 2 moreH: 1, needs 1H: 1, needs 1
        Oxygen is in Group 6: six outer electrons, two short of eight. Each hydrogen has one electron, one short of two.
        
        
        Overlap the shells

Your turn · the shared-pair builder
            Choose how many pairs each bond shares.
          
          0 of 7 built
        
        
          HClCl₂O₂N₂NH₃CH₄CO₂
        
        
          NHHH
          
            
              
                N–H bond
                
                  −
                  0 pairs
                  +
                
              
            
              
                N–H bond
                
                  −
                  0 pairs
                  +
                
              
            
              
                N–H bond
                
                  −
                  0 pairs
                  +
                
              
            
            
              N: 5 of 8H 1: 1 of 2H 2: 1 of 2H 3: 1 of 2
            
            Check the molecule

Most covalent substances are small molecules like these: a fixed number of atoms, strong bonds inside, and separate molecules that are only weakly attracted to each other. Some are very large molecules, such as the polymers in plastic. Some are giant covalent structures, like diamond and sand, where the bonds never stop. The strong bond is always the one between atoms. Sort out which statements believe that.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.4 · Process
        Covalent bonding
        When two atoms both want electrons, neither will give any away. How do they still end up with full shells?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Two hydrogen atoms. One electron each. Both need two.
        Hydrogen gas is not made of single atoms. It is made of H₂ molecules, and pulling one apart takes a lot of energy. Yet each hydrogen atom has only one electron, and a full first shell needs two. Neither atom is a metal, so neither will hand its electron over.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  How can both hydrogen atoms have a full shell at the same time?
  
    
      
        
          A
          They share their two electrons, and both count the pair as their own
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          One gives its electron to the other, making ions
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          They borrow electrons from the air around them
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          They cannot: H₂ has half-empty shells

Two non-metal atoms overlap their outer shells and share a pair of electrons, one from each. Both atoms count the shared pair as their own. The pair sits between the two nuclei and is attracted to both of them, and that attraction holds the atoms together: one shared pair is one covalent bond. Covalent bonds are strong. An atom forms as many bonds as it needs electrons: hydrogen one, oxygen two, nitrogen three, carbon four. Call the next one before you see it.

Worked · water, H₂O

          Step 1 of 3
        
        OHHO: 6 outer, needs 2 moreH: 1, needs 1H: 1, needs 1
        Oxygen is in Group 6: six outer electrons, two short of eight. Each hydrogen has one electron, one short of two.
        
        
        Overlap the shells

Sort out which statements believe that.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.1.5 · Model
        Metallic bonding
        One picture of a metal explains why a copper wire carries current, a pan handle gets hot and gold can be beaten thinner than paper. What is that picture?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A grain of gold, hammered into a sheet the size of a tablecloth.
        Gold-beaters hammer one gram of gold into a sheet close to a square metre in area, only a few hundred atoms thick. It never cracks. Hit a grain of salt, another giant structure of charged particles, and it shatters at the first blow.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  What must be true inside gold for it to bend instead of break?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Its particles can shift past each other without the bonding breaking
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Gold atoms are softer than sodium and chloride ions
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Gold has no charged particles, so nothing repels
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The hammering melts the gold a little at a time

In a metal, every atom gives up its outer electrons. Those electrons do not belong to any one atom any more: they are delocalised, free to move through the whole structure. What is left behind is a regular lattice of positive metal ions, sitting in a sea of delocalised electrons. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and that sea. Before you test the model, check you have the bond in the right place.

!Think again
        “In a metal, each atom is bonded to the atoms next to it.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Describe
  
  
  What is wrong with that description?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The atoms have given up their outer electrons. The bond is between the positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Nothing: metal atoms share electron pairs with their neighbours.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The atoms are bonded to each other by electrons transferred between them.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The ions repel each other, so there is no bond at all.

The electron-sea workbench

              The delocalised electrons drift towards the positive terminalThe positive ions travel along the wireNothing can move: the metal is a solid

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.1–5.2.2.2 · Investigation
        States of matter
        You keep heating a solid, but the thermometer stops rising. Where is the energy going, and how do you find a melting point from messy readings?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Contains Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here · an exam scenario
        A tube of white wax in a hot-water bath.
        A student puts a boiling tube of solid stearic acid, a waxy substance, into a beaker of water at 90 °C. She stirs the wax with the thermometer and reads the temperature every 30 seconds for ten minutes. The water bath never stops heating the tube.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  While the wax is melting, what does the thermometer do?
  
    
      
        
          A
          It keeps rising steadily, because heat keeps going in
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          It stays at about the same temperature until all the wax has melted
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          It falls, because melting takes heat away
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          It rises faster, because liquids heat up more easily

In a solid, particles are packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, they are still close together but randomly arranged, and they move past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and move quickly in all directions. Melting and boiling need energy, because the forces between the particles have to be overcome. The stronger those forces, the more energy it takes, and the higher the melting or boiling point. Run the investigation and watch the energy go.

Higher
            Limits of the model · AQA 5.2.2.1 (HT only)
          
          The particle diagrams you have used draw particles as small, solid, inelastic spheres with nothing between them. Real particles are not solid balls, they are not all spheres, and there are forces between them. The simple model cannot say why one substance melts at 69 °C and another at 801 °C.
          
            
  
    Your call
    Suggest
  
  
  The particle model represents particles as small solid spheres. Suggest one limitation of this model.
  
    
      
        
          A
          It proves that all substances are the same
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          It cannot be used to explain changes of state
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          It shows that particles move, which is incorrect
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          It treats particles as solid, identical spheres and ignores the forces between them (and their real shapes and sizes)

            Limits of the model · AQA 5.2.2.1 (HT only)
          
          The particle diagrams you have used draw particles as small, solid, inelastic spheres with nothing between them. Real particles are not solid balls, they are not all spheres, and there are forces between them. The simple model cannot say why one substance melts at 69 °C and another at 801 °C.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.3 · Contrast
        Properties of ionic compounds
        Salt is made entirely of charged particles, yet a salt crystal will not light a bulb. Melt it, or dissolve it, and it will. What changed?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Two probes, one bulb, a pile of salt crystals.
        Push two carbon probes into a heap of dry salt crystals and connect them to a battery and a bulb. The bulb stays dark. Every crystal is packed with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions: billions of charged particles, right between the probes.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does no current flow through the crystals?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The positive and negative charges cancel out
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Salt has no charged particles in it
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The crystals are not touching the probes properly

A current is a flow of charge, so it needs charged particles that can move. Having charged particles is not enough. In solid sodium chloride every ion is held in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces from all its neighbours. The ions vibrate but stay put. That leaves one question to test: what happens when something sets them free? Compare the solid with each of the other forms, one at a time, and call the bulb first.

        Salt is made entirely of charged particles, yet a salt crystal will not light a bulb. Melt it, or dissolve it, and it will. What changed?

Start here
        Two probes, one bulb, a pile of salt crystals.

          C

          D
          The crystals are not touching the probes properly

A current is a flow of charge, so it needs charged particles that can move. Having charged particles is not enough. In solid sodium chloride every ion is held in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces from all its neighbours. The ions vibrate but stay put. That leaves one question to test: what happens when something sets them free? Compare the solid with each of the other forms, one at a time, and call the bulb first.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.3 · Contrast
        Properties of ionic compounds
        Salt is made entirely of charged particles, yet a salt crystal will not light a bulb. Melt it, or dissolve it, and it will. What changed?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Two probes, one bulb, a pile of salt crystals.
        Push two carbon probes into a heap of dry salt crystals and connect them to a battery and a bulb. The bulb stays dark. Every crystal is packed with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions: billions of charged particles, right between the probes.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does no current flow through the crystals?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The positive and negative charges cancel out
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Salt has no charged particles in it
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The crystals are not touching the probes properly

A current is a flow of charge, so it needs charged particles that can move. Having charged particles is not enough. In solid sodium chloride every ion is held in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces from all its neighbours. The ions vibrate but stay put. That leaves one question to test: what happens when something sets them free? Compare the solid with each of the other forms, one at a time, and call the bulb first.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.4 · Model
        Properties of small molecules
        Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid, yet every one of them is a pair of atoms held by one covalent bond. What sets the difference?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A kettle of water. A bubble of steam.
        Water boils at 100 °C. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs an electric current running through it for minutes, or a temperature of thousands of degrees. Both processes start with the same H₂O molecules.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  What is inside a bubble of steam?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Whole water molecules, spread far apart
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Hydrogen and oxygen gases
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Hot air that was dissolved in the water
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Nothing: a steam bubble is empty

A small molecule is a fixed group of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds: H₂O, CH₄, Cl₂. Between one molecule and the next there are only weak intermolecular forces. So a small-molecule substance has two kinds of attraction in it, one strong and one weak, and only the weak one decides when it melts or boils. Heat some molecules and see which gives way.

The two-forces model
            Pick a molecule. Turn up the heat.
          
          0 of 5 molecules heated
        
        
          H₂OCH₄Cl₂Br₂I₂
        
        
          
          
            Temperature
            
            20 °C · liquid
            water · melts 0 °C · boils 100 °C
            Liquid: some intermolecular forces have been overcome; molecules slide past each other.

The bigger the molecule, the stronger the intermolecular forces between neighbours, and the more energy it takes to separate them. That is the whole pattern down Group 7, and it is why most small-molecule substances are gases or liquids at room temperature while a few large ones are solids. Small molecules also never conduct electricity: a molecule has no overall charge, and there are no free electrons or ions.

A small molecule is a fixed group of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds: H₂O, CH₄, Cl₂. Between one molecule and the next there are only weak intermolecular forces. AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.5 · Classify
        Polymers
        Ethene is a gas. Poly(ethene), made of nothing but ethene joined up, is a solid carrier bag. Can you tell a polymer from every other structure at a glance, and say why it is solid?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Contains Triple
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        Same atoms. One is a gas, one is a carrier bag.
        An ethene molecule, C₂H₄, has six atoms. It boils at −104 °C. A single molecule of poly(ethene) in a carrier bag is a chain of many thousands of carbon atoms, each with two hydrogens. The bag stays solid until it softens at over 100 °C. Both substances contain only strong covalent bonds inside their molecules.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature when ethene is a gas?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Its molecules are so large that the forces between them are much stronger
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Joining up the molecules made the covalent bonds stronger
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Poly(ethene) is a giant covalent structure
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Poly(ethene) has ions in it

A polymer is a very large molecule made of many small units joined in a long chain. Inside each chain, atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds. Between chains there are only intermolecular forces, just as between small molecules, but because the molecules are so large those forces are relatively strong. That is why polymers are solids at room temperature. An exam diagram rarely names the structure. You have to recognise it.

            What structure does the diagram show?

            Small moleculesPolymerGiant covalentGiant ionicGiant metallic

!Think again
        “A polymer chain is so huge that it must be a giant covalent structure, like diamond.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Compare
  
  
  Poly(ethene) softens at about 120 °C. Diamond survives above 3500 °C. What explains the gap?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Melting poly(ethene) overcomes intermolecular forces between chains; melting diamond means breaking strong covalent bonds.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Poly(ethene)’s covalent bonds are weaker than diamond’s.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Diamond is a larger molecule than poly(ethene).
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Poly(ethene) is not pure carbon, so it is weaker.

Triple
            Addition polymerisation · AQA 4.7.3.1 (chemistry only)
          
          Open the double bond. Join the chain.
          Ethene has a C=C double bond. In addition polymerisation one bond of each double bond opens and the monomers link into a chain. Before you build one, commit.
          
            
              Eight ethene molecules (48 atoms) join into one chain. How many atoms are lost?
              
                0816
              
            
          
          
          Thermosoftening polymers, like poly(ethene), are separate chains: heat overcomes the forces between chains and they soften and melt. Thermosetting polymers have cross-links, covalent bonds between chains, so they do not melt when heated.

Command words in this lesson
        
          IdentifyName the structure from the diagram. Look for brackets and n, or bonds running off the edge.
          ExplainLarge molecules, relatively strong forces between them, so more energy to overcome.
          CompareName what is overcome in each: forces between molecules, or covalent bonds.

        Polymers are very large molecules. The intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, so they are solids at room temperature, but they are molecules, not giant covalent structures.

        Don't call a polymer a giant covalent structure. It is a large molecule whose chains are held to each other by weak intermolecular forces — that is why it melts far below diamond, where strong covalent bonds run all the way through. That force difference is where the comparison marks are.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.6 · 5.2.3.1–5.2.3.3 · Contrast
        Giant covalent structures
        A diamond and a pencil lead are both pure carbon. One is the hardest natural material known; the other smears on paper and conducts electricity. What one difference does all that?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A drill bit and a pencil. Both carbon.
        Diamond-tipped drills cut through granite. Graphite, the grey “lead” in a pencil, is so soft it rubs off onto paper and is used to lubricate locks, yet it carries a current well enough to be used as electrodes. Neither melts until it is hotter than 3500 °C.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Same element, same very high melting point. What differs?
  
    
      
        
          A
          How the carbon atoms are bonded to each other
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Graphite has impurities that make it soft
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Diamond is carbon under pressure, so its atoms are smaller
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Graphite is a metal and diamond is not

In a giant covalent structure every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds, and the bonding runs on through the whole solid. There are no separate molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome. Melting means breaking huge numbers of strong covalent bonds, which is why these substances have very high melting points. Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide (sand) are all built this way. The difference between diamond and graphite comes down to one count.

Diamond against graphite
            Count the bonds. Then call each property.

    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  Graphite conducts, but carbon is a non-metal. Where do its mobile electrons come from?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Each carbon bonds to only three others, so one outer electron per atom is delocalised and can move along the layers.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Graphite contains metal atoms mixed in with the carbon.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The layers are made of carbon ions that carry the current.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Graphite has a sea of electrons, so it has metallic bonding.

Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong and conducts, for the same reasons as graphite’s layers. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon with hollow shapes, built from rings of carbon atoms, usually hexagons with some pentagons. The first found was buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, a hollow sphere. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with a very high length-to-diameter ratio. These are core content on every route.

  Graphene, C₆₀ or nanotube?
  Each statement describes one of the three. Decide from the structure.

      A hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms.
    
      Used to reinforce materials such as tennis rackets.
    
      Could be used in thin, flexible electronics because it conducts and is very strong.

        In diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds; in graphite, three, leaving one delocalised electron per atom and layers held only by weak forces. Every property follows from that count.

AQA Chemistry 5.2.2.6 · 5.2.3.1–5.2.3.3 · Contrast
        Giant covalent structures
        A diamond and a pencil lead are both pure carbon. One is the hardest natural material known; the other smears on paper and conducts electricity. What one difference does all that?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A drill bit and a pencil. Both carbon.
        Diamond-tipped drills cut through granite. Graphite, the grey “lead” in a pencil, is so soft it rubs off onto paper and is used to lubricate locks, yet it carries a current well enough to be used as electrodes. Neither melts until it is hotter than 3500 °C.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Same element, same very high melting point. What differs?
  
    
      
        
          A
          How the carbon atoms are bonded to each other
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Graphite has impurities that make it soft
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Diamond is carbon under pressure, so its atoms are smaller
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Graphite is a metal and diamond is not

In a giant covalent structure every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds, and the bonding runs on through the whole solid. There are no separate molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome. Melting means breaking huge numbers of strong covalent bonds, which is why these substances have very high melting points. Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide (sand) are all built this way. The difference between diamond and graphite comes down to one count.

Diamond against graphite

Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong and conducts, for the same reasons as graphite’s layers. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon with hollow shapes, built from rings of carbon atoms, usually hexagons with some pentagons. The first found was buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, a hollow sphere. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with a very high length-to-diameter ratio. These are core content on every route.

        Metals and alloys
        Pure gold bends between your fingers, and pure iron is too soft for a bridge. Mix in a few atoms of something else and the metal turns hard. How can adding a little of another element change so much?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Contains Triple
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        24-carat gold scratches. 18-carat gold lasts a lifetime.
        Pure, 24-carat gold is so soft that a ring made from it dents and scratches in weeks. Most wedding rings are 18-carat: three parts gold mixed with one part of other metals such as copper and silver. They keep their shape for decades.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why would mixing in other metal atoms make gold harder?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The different-sized atoms get in the way of the layers moving
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The copper and gold react to make a hard compound
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Copper atoms are harder than gold atoms
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The extra metal fills gaps, so there is less space to bend into

In a pure metal, all the atoms are the same size, so they pack in regular layers. When a force is applied, whole layers can slide over each other and the metal bends: that is why pure metals such as gold, copper, iron and aluminium are soft. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, usually other metals. The added atoms are a different size. Mix some in and test what the layers do.

The alloy mixer

  A solid copper wire carries current every day. What is wrong with the claim?
  
    
      
        
          A
          A metal’s delocalised electrons are already free to move in the solid. Ionic compounds need melting because their charge carriers are ions, locked in place.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          Nothing: copper wires warm up, which melts them slightly so they conduct.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          Metals conduct because their positive ions move, and ions can move in solid metals.
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Metals do not really conduct as solids; they need a coating.

Build the chain
    Why is an alloy harder than the pure metal?
  
  The classic 3-mark explanation. Four links in order; two are false.

          The distorted layers cannot slide over each other easily, so the alloy is harder.
        
          In a pure metal, the atoms are all the same size and arranged in regular layers.
        
          The alloy forms stronger ionic bonds between its metals.
        
          In an alloy, atoms of a different size distort the layers.

AQA Chemistry 4.2.4 (chemistry only) · Quantitative
        Nanoparticles
        Gold is yellow and unreactive. Grind it into particles a few nanometres across and it turns red and becomes a catalyst. Same atoms. What changed, and can you calculate it?
        
          Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A red glass window, coloured with gold.
        Medieval glassmakers turned windows ruby-red by stirring in a trace of gold. The gold spreads through the glass as particles around 25 nm across, too small to see. A gold ring and the red glass contain exactly the same kind of atom.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does gold behave so differently at this size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          A far bigger share of its atoms are at the surface
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The gold has reacted with the glass to form a new compound
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The atoms themselves become smaller
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Heat from the furnace changes gold into another element

Nanoscience is about structures 1 to 100 nm across: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, a billionth of a metre. A nanoparticle holds only a few hundred atoms; an atom is about 0.1 nm across. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5), which are 100 to 2500 nm across, and much smaller than coarse particles (PM10), the dust of 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m. Sorting a particle means getting every size into the same unit first.

Sort by size
  Coarse, fine or nano?
  Convert each size to nanometres first. 1 µm = 1000 nm.
  Tap a card, then tap the box it belongs in. Tap a placed card to take it back.
  
    
      A silver particle in a wound dressing, 1 × 10⁻⁸ m
    
      A titanium dioxide particle in sun cream, 20 nm
    
      Sea-salt spray, 8 µm
    
      A diesel soot particle, 0.5 µm across

AQA Chemistry 4.2.4 (chemistry only) · Quantitative
        Nanoparticles
        Gold is yellow and unreactive. Grind it into particles a few nanometres across and it turns red and becomes a catalyst. Same atoms. What changed, and can you calculate it?
        
          Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A red glass window, coloured with gold.
        Medieval glassmakers turned windows ruby-red by stirring in a trace of gold. The gold spreads through the glass as particles around 25 nm across, too small to see. A gold ring and the red glass contain exactly the same kind of atom.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does gold behave so differently at this size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          A far bigger share of its atoms are at the surface
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The gold has reacted with the glass to form a new compound
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The atoms themselves become smaller
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Heat from the furnace changes gold into another element

Nanoscience is about structures 1 to 100 nm across: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, a billionth of a metre. A nanoparticle holds only a few hundred atoms; an atom is about 0.1 nm across. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5), which are 100 to 2500 nm across, and much smaller than coarse particles (PM10), the dust of 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m. Sorting a particle means getting every size into the same unit first.

  Coarse, fine or nano?

        Coarse · PM10 
        
      
    
      
        Fine · PM2.5 
        
      
    
      
        Nanoparticle

            Make the particle smaller. Watch the surface win.
          
          1 of 4 sizes viewed

              It increases 10 timesIt decreases 10 timesIt increases 100 timesIt increases 1000 times

!Think again
        “Red nanogold must be a different substance from yellow gold.”
        
  
    Spot the flaw
    Explain
  
  
  What really changes when gold becomes nanoparticles?
  
    
      
        
          A
          Only the scale. The atoms are the same gold atoms, but far more of them sit on the surface.
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The gold atoms bond to each other differently, making a new substance.
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The gold loses electrons and becomes gold ions.

            Rearranged, to find the side from a ratio.

            L in nm gives the ratio in nm⁻¹ (per nanometre). Convert every length to nm before you insert it.

        Gold is yellow and unreactive. Grind it into particles a few nanometres across and it turns red and becomes a catalyst. Same atoms. What changed, and can you calculate it?

Start here

AQA Chemistry 4.2.4 (chemistry only) · Quantitative
        Nanoparticles
        Gold is yellow and unreactive. Grind it into particles a few nanometres across and it turns red and becomes a catalyst. Same atoms. What changed, and can you calculate it?
        
          Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route
            
              Combined FoundationCombined HigherTriple FoundationTriple Higher
            
          
        
        
        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A red glass window, coloured with gold.
        Medieval glassmakers turned windows ruby-red by stirring in a trace of gold. The gold spreads through the glass as particles around 25 nm across, too small to see. A gold ring and the red glass contain exactly the same kind of atom.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  Why does gold behave so differently at this size?
  
    
      
        
          A
          A far bigger share of its atoms are at the surface
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The gold has reacted with the glass to form a new compound
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The atoms themselves become smaller
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Heat from the furnace changes gold into another element

Nanoscience is about structures 1 to 100 nm across: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, a billionth of a metre. A nanoparticle holds only a few hundred atoms; an atom is about 0.1 nm across. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5), which are 100 to 2500 nm across, and much smaller than coarse particles (PM10), the dust of 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m. Sorting a particle means getting every size into the same unit first.

Equation

        Series and parallel circuits
        Change one resistor in a circuit and every reading can move. Can you predict which ones, and which way, before the meters tell you?
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher
          Route

Start here · an exam scenario
        A 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor, one 12 V battery.
        A? AR₁4 ΩR₂8 Ω12 VV? V
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  The two resistors are in series. Which one has the bigger potential difference across it?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The 8 Ω resistor
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The 4 Ω resistor
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          They share it equally, 6 V each
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Each has the full 12 V

In a series circuit there is one loop. The same current passes through every component, and the battery's potential difference is shared between them: bigger resistance, bigger share. Resistances add: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂. In a parallel circuit each branch is connected straight across the battery, so every branch has the full potential difference, and the branch currents add up to the current from the battery. Now change the circuit, one part at a time.

AQA Physics 6.2.2 · System
        Series and parallel circuits
        Change one resistor in a circuit and every reading can move. Can you predict which ones, and which way, before the meters tell you?

Start here · an exam scenario
        A 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor, one 12 V battery.
        A? AR₁4 ΩR₂8 Ω12 VV? V
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  The two resistors are in series. Which one has the bigger potential difference across it?
  
    
      
        
          A
          The 8 Ω resistor
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          The 4 Ω resistor
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          They share it equally, 6 V each
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          Each has the full 12 V

In a series circuit there is one loop. The same current passes through every component, and the battery's potential difference is shared between them: bigger resistance, bigger share. Resistances add: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂. In a parallel circuit each branch is connected straight across the battery, so every branch has the full potential difference, and the branch currents add up to the current from the battery. Now change the circuit, one part at a time.

AQA Physics 6.2.1.4 · Required practical
        Resistors and I–V characteristics
        Double the potential difference across a component. Does the current double? For a resistor, a lamp and a diode, find out, and learn the method AQA will ask you to describe.
        
          Combined · Triple
          Foundation · Higher

          Route

        Draft — not yet science-reviewed.

Start here
        A bulb takes a big gulp of current, then settles.
        Switch on an old filament bulb and, for the first fraction of a second, it draws several times more current than it does once it is glowing. Filament bulbs usually blow at the moment they are switched on, not while they are lit.
        
          
  
    Commit first
    
  
  
  What must be different about the cold filament?
  
    
      
        
          A
          A cold filament has a lower resistance than a hot one
        
      
    
      
        
          B
          A cold filament has a higher resistance
        
      
    
      
        
          C
          The battery pushes harder at first
        
      
    
      
        
          D
          The glass has to warm up before light gets out

Required practical · the AQA method
        Build the circuit. Change the p.d. Measure the current.
        
          Aresistor6 Vvariable resistorV
          
            Connect the component in series with an ammeter, a variable resistor and the battery. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the component.
            Use the variable resistor to set the p.d. Record the p.d. and the current.
            Repeat for a range of p.d. values, switching off between readings so the component does not heat up.
            Reverse the connections to the battery and repeat, to get negative values.
            Plot current (y-axis) against p.d. (x-axis) for each component.
          
        
        Risks. A filament lamp gets hot enough to burn: do not touch it while it is on, and let it cool. A resistor carrying a large current also warms up, which changes its resistance: keep currents low and switch off between readings.
